screens.title: What is a CDN and how CloudFront implements it
screens.narratorSegment: A Content Delivery Network is a geographically distributed system of servers that caches and serves content from locations near users. This reduces the time it takes for a user to receive content because the request often lands at a nearby edge location instead of traveling to a distant origin server. CloudFront is Amazon's managed CDN that implements these ideas across AWS's global edge network. In practice, a viewer's DNS resolves to an edge location; the edge checks its cache and either serves a cached object, a cache hit, or fetches the object from the configured origin on a cache miss. This basic flow lowers latency and reduces origin load. A common misconception is that a CDN simply duplicates origin content statically; in reality, caching is configurable. You define what to cache, for how long, and which headers or query strings to forward. For example, caching an image for long durations is usually safe, while an A P I response that carries user personalization requires forwarding headers and short or zero TTL. Understanding this distinction lets you balance performance and correctness. Takeaway: the CDN's role is not only speed — it's controlled placement of content with precise rules so that cached copies serve correct, secure responses.

keyIdea.text: A CDN caches content at edge locations to serve users faster; CloudFront provides configurable caching and delivery features to balance speed and correctness.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › What is a CDN
Definition

CDN concept explained

A CDN caches content at edge locations to reduce round-trip time and origin load while letting you control caching behavior.

Why it matters
Lower latency for users worldwide and decreased load on origin servers improves availability and cost-efficiency.
Common misconception
CDNs are not purely static copies; caching rules, TTLs, and header forwarding control freshness and correctness.
Key Takeaway

A CDN acts as an intelligent cache network; configure it to serve correct and fresh content, not just faster content.

Request lifecycle (illustrative)
Viewer DNS → Edge location → cache check. Hit: serve from edge. Miss: fetch from origin, cache, then serve.
Concrete example
An image stored in S3 is cached at an edge. When many users request it, they get a fast cache hit instead of repeated origin requests.
Check your understanding
When would you prefer a short TTL? Think of personalized API responses.
Pro tip
Start with conservative caching for dynamic paths and increase TTLs for stable static assets.

screens.title: CloudFront Distribution: origins, behaviors, and cache policies
screens.narratorSegment: A CloudFront distribution is the configuration object that ties origins to delivery rules. At a minimum it specifies one or more origins — the sources of content like S3 buckets or ALBs — and cache behaviors that route requests to those origins based on path patterns. Cache behaviors determine which origin handles a request and which cache policy applies. A cache policy specifies TTLs, whether to forward query strings, headers, and cookies, and whether to compress objects at the edge. This split gives you granular control: for static assets you can choose long TTLs and minimal header forwarding, while for A P I paths you can forward headers and set a short or zero TTL. A common pitfall is misconfigured behavior precedence: the most specific path pattern wins, so place /api/* above /*. Consider security settings at the behavior level too — viewer protocol policies enforce HTTPS. Concrete example: a distribution with two origins, one pointing to my-website-bucket and another to my-api-alb, defines a default behavior for the website and a specific /api/* behavior with TTL=0 and header forwarding. This design keeps content fresh while accelerating static files.

keyIdea.text: Origins supply content; behaviors route requests by path; cache policies control TTLs and what is forwarded to the origin.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Distribution Components
Definition

Origins, Behaviors, Cache Policies

Use behaviors to map path patterns to origins and choose cache policies to control TTLs and forwarding.

Behavior precedence
More specific path patterns take priority; order your behaviors accordingly.
Forwarding decisions
Forward headers/cookies only when necessary to avoid cache fragmentation and stale content.
Key Takeaway

Separate static and dynamic paths into different behaviors to apply appropriate caching and forwarding rules.

Concrete distribution example
Origins
my-website-bucket (S3), my-api-alb (ALB)
Behaviors
Default /* → S3 with TTL 24 hours; /api/* → ALB with TTL=0 and all headers forwarded.
Cache policy
Use a caching policy with selective header forwarding and appropriate TTLs per behavior.
Common mistake
Caching dynamic API responses for long TTLs can return stale, incorrect data to users.
Pro tip
Use separate cache policies for static and dynamic behaviors to keep rules explicit and auditable.

screens.title: Origins: S3 vs ALB/EC2
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFront supports multiple origin types: S3 for static assets and ALB/EC2 for dynamic or application-backed responses. S3 is ideal for public static files like images, C S S, and H T M L because objects are immutable and safe to cache long-term. For S3 origins, configure Origin Access Control so the bucket denies public access and only CloudFront can fetch objects. ALB or EC2 origins are appropriate for APIs or dynamic content that require server-side computation or personalization. When using ALB/EC2, CloudFront fetches via the origin's public endpoint and you must decide what to forward — query strings, headers, and cookies — so the origin can respond correctly. A useful comparison: S3 origin with long TTLs reduces origin calls and is simple to secure with OAC; ALB/EC2 origin needs careful header forwarding and often short TTLs. A misconception is that S3 cannot serve dynamic content — it can only serve static files; dynamic responses must come from compute origins. Concrete example: host index. html and assets in S3, and point A P I paths to an ALB; enforce OAC on the S3 bucket to prevent direct access. The right origin choice helps you balance performance, security, and freshness.

keyIdea.text: Use S3 for immutable static content with OAC; use ALB/EC2 for dynamic or personalized responses that require server logic.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Origins: S3 vs ALB/EC2

Origin comparison

Match origin type to content characteristics and security needs.

S3 origin
Best for static files. Use Origin Access Control to block direct public access and allow CloudFront only.
ALB / EC2 origin
For APIs or dynamic content. Decide which headers, cookies, and query strings need forwarding.
Key Takeaway

Choose S3 for cache-friendly static content and ALB/EC2 when server logic or personalization is required.

Concrete setup scenario
Place index.html and images in S3 and point API paths to an ALB. Create two behaviors: default for S3 with long TTL, and /api/* for ALB with zero TTL and header forwarding.
Common mistake
Allowing public access to S3 without OAC exposes content and bypasses CloudFront's caching and security layers.
Pro tip
Use the most specific path patterns before the default to ensure API routes are matched correctly.

screens.title: Request lifecycle: cache hit vs cache miss
screens.narratorSegment: To reason about performance and origin load, trace the request lifecycle. Step one: DNS resolves the distribution domain to an edge location closest to the viewer. Step two: the edge location checks for the requested object in its cache. If the object exists and is not expired, that's a cache hit — CloudFront returns the object immediately and the origin is not contacted. If the object is missing or expired, that's a cache miss — CloudFront forwards the request to the configured origin, possibly running Lambda@Edge on the way, receives the response, caches it according to the behavior's cache policy, and then delivers it to the viewer. Misconfigurations often cause unnecessary misses: forwarding unnecessary headers or query strings fragments the the cache, and setting very short TTLs turns what could be hits into frequent origin requests. Concrete example: a popular image with long TTL becomes a hit at many edges; an A P I endpoint with TTL=0 always misses and queries the origin. Monitoring the cache hit ratio helps you confirm expected behavior. Ask yourself: for each path pattern, do you prefer freshness or origin throttling? That choice determines caching rules.

keyIdea.text: A request resolves to an edge, which decides hit or miss. Misses fetch and then cache the response, hits serve directly from the edge.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Request Lifecycle
Process Flow

Cache hit vs cache miss

A short numbered sequence explains the lifecycle and what each step implies for performance and origin traffic.

1. DNS → Edge
Viewer resolves distribution domain to nearest edge location IP.
2. Cache check
Edge checks local cache for object and TTL validity.
3a. Hit
Serve from edge immediately; origin not contacted.
3b. Miss
Fetch from origin, possibly run Lambda@Edge, cache response, then serve.
Concrete example
An image requested worldwide is a hit at many edges after the first miss; an API with TTL=0 always causes misses.
Common mistake
Forwarding too many headers or query strings fragments the cache and converts hits into misses.
Key Takeaway

Design behaviors to maximize hits where possible and accept misses where correctness demands freshness.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Create a CloudFront distribution

Quick setup steps

  1. Create an S3 bucket and keep "Block all public access" enabled.
  2. Upload index.html and any assets to the bucket.
  3. Create a CloudFront distribution, select the S3 origin, and create Origin Access Control.
  4. Apply the provided bucket policy to allow the OAC to fetch objects.
  5. Wait for distribution deployment and verify via the distribution domain.
Key Takeaway

OAC is essential to prevent users from bypassing CloudFront and directly accessing S3 content.

Starter index.html (upload to S3)
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8" />
  <title>CloudFront Demo</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello from CloudFront!</h1>
  <p>This content is served via Amazon S3 and CloudFront.</p>
</body>
</html>
Check
After deployment, visit https://YOUR_DISTRIBUTION_DOMAIN_NAME/index.html and verify content loads.
Verify OAC
Attempting to open the S3 object URL should return Access Denied if OAC and policy are correct.

screens.title: Origin Access Control and protecting S3 origins
screens.narratorSegment: Origin Access Control is the recommended way to ensure CloudFront is the only path to your S3 content. With OAC enabled, CloudFront signs origin requests and you update the S3 bucket policy to allow access from that CloudFront identity. This prevents end users from bypassing the CDN by calling the S3 public URL directly. In the hands-on example you configured OAC and applied the bucket policy; verifying that the S3 URL returns Access Denied confirms the control is in place. A misconception is that making S3 public and relying on CloudFront is sufficient; a public bucket can be accessed directly unless you restrict it. Another common error is failing to update the bucket policy after creating the OAC — CloudFront will not be able to fetch objects until permissions are corrected. Use signed URLs or signed cookies on top of OAC when you need per-user access control for private content. Key practical step: always check S3 permissions after creating the control and test the distribution domain and direct S3 access to confirm the intended restriction. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: OAC plus an updated bucket policy ensures S3 objects are only retrieveable through CloudFront, preventing bypass and enforcing CDN rules.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Origin Access Control (OAC)

Origin Access Control

OAC ensures that S3 objects are only accessible via CloudFront by updating bucket policy to allow CloudFront's origin identity.

Why use OAC
Prevents direct public access and enforces CDN policy, preserving performance and security guarantees.
Common mistake
Not updating the bucket policy after creating OAC leaves CloudFront unable to fetch objects or leaves the bucket still publicly accessible.
Key Takeaway

Always configure OAC and update the S3 bucket policy to restrict direct access and validate via both the distribution URL and the S3 URL.

Scenario
After creating OAC, CloudFront provides a JSON policy. Apply it to your S3 bucket's permissions so only the CloudFront origin identity can GET objects. Then verify direct S3 access is denied and the CloudFront URL serves content.
Check
Confirm S3 URL returns Access Denied and distribution domain serves the same object.
Pro tip
Use CloudFront's origin identity details exactly as provided in the bucket policy to avoid permission errors.

screens.title: Cache policies, TTLs, and forwarding rules
screens.narratorSegment: Cache policies determine exactly what CloudFront caches and for how long. The Time-to-Live value specifies how long an object is considered fresh at the edge before it must be revalidated or refetched. Policies also specify whether to forward query strings, headers, and cookies to the origin. Cache policy essentials

Choose TTLs and decide which fields to forward. These decisions directly affect cache hit ratios and correctness.

Long TTLs
Best for immutable static assets like images and compiled CSS.
Short or zero TTLs
Used for APIs or highly dynamic responses where freshness is critical.

Optimize for cacheability: minimize forwarded fields for static content and only forward what's required for dynamic content.

Use a CachingOptimized policy for static assets with long TTL; use a policy that forwards headers, cookies, and query strings for /api/* and set TTL=0.

screens.title: Signed URLs, signed cookies, and HTTPS
screens.narratorSegment: When you need to restrict access to specific objects, CloudFront supports signed URLs and signed cookies. Signed URLs grant a time-limited, per-object access token, while signed cookies let you grant access to multiple objects for a viewer session. Use these mechanisms when the content must remain private and only certain users should retrieve it. In addition, enforce HTTPS by choosing the viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and add custom certificates through AWS Certificate Manager when you use your own domain. Another layer of protection is AWS WAF integration to block common web exploits at the edge. A common misconception is that signed URLs replace Origin Access Control; they serve different purposes. OAC restricts direct S3 access to CloudFront only, while signed URLs control which viewers are permitted to fetch a given resource through CloudFront. For private content, use OAC together with signed URLs or signed cookies to ensure CloudFront is the gatekeeper and the gate enforces user-level authorization. Signed URLs, signed cookies, and HTTPS means use signed urls or signed cookies for viewer-level restrictions; use oac to restrict origin access and https/waf to secure transport and block threats.. In practical terms, controlling access to private content and enforcing secure transport. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Access and transport security

Combine OAC, signed URLs/cookies, HTTPS, and WAF to secure both origin access and viewer access.

Signed URLs vs Signed Cookies
Use signed URLs for single-object access and signed cookies for session-level access to multiple objects.
Transport security
Enforce HTTPS via viewer protocol policies and use ACM-managed certificates for custom domains.
Key Takeaway

Combine origin and viewer controls: OAC stops bypass, signed credentials control who can view, and HTTPS/WAF protect transport and requests.

Concrete example
Protect premium downloads with signed URLs and block common threats with WAF rules attached to the distribution. Use OAC to ensure the objects are only served through CloudFront.
Common mistake
Relying on bucket ACLs or public access alone without OAC leaves gaps; use policy-based control instead.

Use short expiration for signed URLs and rotate keys regularly if you implement custom signing logic.

screens.title: Lambda@Edge: run code at CloudFront edge
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda@Edge allows you to run small pieces of serverless code at CloudFront edge locations in response to events in the request lifecycle. This can transform requests, add or remove headers, perform A/B testing, or implement custom routing logic before a request reaches your origin. Because the code runs at the edge, you can reduce origin calls and add personalization closer to the user. Use Lambda@Edge for lightweight transformations; a misconception is to push heavy computation to the edge — edge functions should be fast and small. Typical uses include rewriting URLs, adding security headers, or deciding which origin to query based on cookies. Keep in mind that debugging edge functions is different from typical server-side code and require careful testing. Concrete example: use an origin-request function that inspects a cookie to route traffic to a feature-flag origin bucket. When using Lambda@Edge, remember to consider its impact on cacheability — modifying headers or body content can affect the cache key and reduce hits. Design functions to preserve cache-friendly behavior where possible. Lambda@Edge: run code at CloudFront edge means lambda@edge enables lightweight request/response transformations at the edge, useful for personalization and routing while keeping latency low.. Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Lambda@Edge

Lambda@Edge overview

Run serverless functions at CloudFront events to modify requests and responses without hitting your origin.

Use cases
URL rewrites, header injection, A/B testing, custom authorization, and origin routing logic.
Design caution
Keep functions small and fast; heavy computation or large state is unsuitable for edge functions.
Key Takeaway

Lambda@Edge adds powerful customization at the edge but requires careful design to avoid reducing cache efficiency or increasing latency.

Concrete example
An origin-request function examines a feature-flag cookie and rewrites the request host header to route to a blue or green origin, enabling edge-based traffic splitting without touching the origin application.
Common mistake
Altering responses in ways that differ per viewer can fragment caches and cause a drop in hit ratios.

Document which headers or cookies your edge functions rely on to keep forwarding rules explicit and predictable.

screens.title: Monitoring cache hit ratio and invalidations
screens.narratorSegment: Operational health of a CloudFront deployment relies on observability and careful invalidation practices. Monitor metrics like cache hit ratio, origin request rate, and edge latency. A low cache hit ratio indicates either excessive forwarding, too many unique cache keys, or inadequate TTLs. Use CloudFront metrics and logs to identify the paths that cause misses and adjust cache policies or behavior rules accordingly. When content changes and must be refreshed before TTL expiry, use invalidation requests to remove objects from edge caches. Invalidations are powerful but can be costly if used excessively, so prefer cache-busting strategies like object versioning when possible. For example, update an asset name from logo. png to logo. v2. png so edges fetch the new object without invalidations. A common misconception is to rely solely on invalidations for frequent content changes; instead, design your deployment to minimize the need for invalidations by using versioned asset names and appropriate TTLs. The result is lower origin load, predictable performance, and controlled freshness. Monitoring cache hit ratio and invalidations means measure hit ratios and origin requests, use invalidation sparingly, and prefer versioned assets to maintain performance and freshness.. In practical terms, maintain performance and freshness with observability and targeted invalidations. Observability and invalidations

Track cache hit ratio and origin requests; invalidate intentionally and prefer versioning to refresh assets.

Metrics to watch
Cache hit ratio, origin request rate, and edge latency reveal delivery health.
Invalidation guidance
Use invalidations for urgent updates but prefer versioned filenames to avoid frequent invalidations.
Key Takeaway

Use monitoring to detect cache inefficiencies and plan invalidations sparingly; version assets to reduce operational cost.

Concrete example
If a CSS file changes frequently during development, serve it with a short TTL or use a versioned filename like styles.v3.css, then update references in HTML to avoid mass invalidations.
Check
If cache hit ratio drops, inspect forwarded fields and unique cache keys that cause fragmentation.
Pro tip
Automate cache invalidation only for critical paths; otherwise update asset names during builds.

screens.title: What to Remember — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important terms you need to remember. A Content Delivery Network distributes cached content at edge locations to reduce latency and origin load. A CloudFront distribution is the configuration that ties origins to cache behaviors and policies. An origin is the source of your content — for example, an S3 bucket or an ALB. Origin Access Control prevents direct public access to S3 so CloudFront is the only route to objects. These pieces form the foundation of secure and performant content delivery. Keep these definitions in mind when you design distributions: they describe who serves content, who accesses it, and the rules that determine freshness. As you practice with the hands-on setup, recall these concepts to guide your architecture and to avoid the common errors we discussed earlier.

fullNarratorScript:
Today you'll explore how Amazon CloudFront speeds up and secures web delivery by caching content at edge locations. We'll connect the core ideas — origins, cache behaviors, and cache policies — to real setup steps and decisions you'll make when serving static assets or dynamic APIs. You'll see why caching at geographically distributed edges reduces latency, how CloudFront decides when to forward requests to your origin, and how Origin Access Control prevents users from bypassing the CDN. A short example will show a single distribution serving an S3-hosted website and an A P I behind a load balancer, with separate cache behaviors for each. We'll also highlight common pitfalls — like caching dynamic responses too long or forgetting to forward headers — and how to avoid them. By the end of this lesson you will be able to describe the request lifecycle, configure basic cache behaviors, and choose security controls that keep your origin private while still letting CloudFront serve content efficiently.

Over the next screens you'll build practical skills around CloudFront. First, you'll understand the core principle of a CDN — placing cached copies of content at geographically distributed edge locations to lower latency. You will be able to describe the components of a CloudFront distribution: origins, cache behaviors, and cache policies, and why those parts matter when designing for performance and correctness. You'll also learn how to configure a basic web distribution to serve content from an S3 bucket or an EC2/ALB origin, including the crucial steps to restrict direct S3 access. Finally, you'll examine the request lifecycle to tell the difference between a cache hit and a cache miss and how that affects origin load. Each objective pairs a short scenario and a small visual mnemonic so you remember the configuration choices and their impact.

This second objectives slide expands the chapter's practical skillset. You will identify common CloudFront use cases beyond static sites, such as streaming media, dynamic content acceleration, and A P I fronting. You'll learn how to choose a caching strategy — when to cache aggressively and when to forward headers or set short TTLs so personalization and freshness are preserved. We'll also emphasize origin security: configuring Origin Access Control so your S3 bucket denies direct public access and only permits CloudFront. Finally, you will gain the habit of monitoring cache hit ratios and using invalidation judiciously to keep content fresh without excessive origin load. For each objective you'll get a short skill check and a mnemonic to help you recall the configuration trade-offs during real deployments. Learning Objectives — Practical Extensions means translate distribution configuration into real use cases: streaming, apis, secure s3 access, and monitoring to balance freshness and performance.. In practical terms, apply these patterns to real-world distribution design. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Content Delivery Network is a geographically distributed system of servers that caches and serves content from locations near users. This reduces the time it takes for a user to receive content because the request often lands at a nearby edge location instead of traveling to a distant origin server. CloudFront is Amazon's managed CDN that implements these ideas across AWS's global edge network. In practice, a viewer's DNS resolves to an edge location; the edge checks its cache and either serves a cached object, a cache hit, or fetches the object from the configured origin on a cache miss. This basic flow lowers latency and reduces origin load. A common misconception is that a CDN simply duplicates origin content statically; in reality, caching is configurable. You define what to cache, for how long, and which headers or query strings to forward. For example, caching an image for long durations is usually safe, while an A P I response that carries user personalization requires forwarding headers and short or zero TTL. Understanding this distinction lets you balance performance and correctness. Takeaway: the CDN's role is not only speed — it's controlled placement of content with precise rules so that cached copies serve correct, secure responses.

A CloudFront distribution is the configuration object that ties origins to delivery rules. At a minimum it specifies one or more origins — the sources of content like S3 buckets or ALBs — and cache behaviors that route requests to those origins based on path patterns. Cache behaviors determine which origin handles a request and which cache policy applies. A cache policy specifies TTLs, whether to forward query strings, headers, and cookies, and whether to compress objects at the edge. This split gives you granular control: for static assets you can choose long TTLs and minimal header forwarding, while for A P I paths you can forward headers and set a short or zero TTL. A common pitfall is misconfigured behavior precedence: the most specific path pattern wins, so place /api/* above /*. Consider security settings at the behavior level too — viewer protocol policies enforce HTTPS. Concrete example: a distribution with two origins, one pointing to my-website-bucket and another to my-api-alb, defines a default behavior for the website and a specific /api/* behavior with TTL=0 and header forwarding. This design keeps content fresh while accelerating static files.

CloudFront supports multiple origin types: S3 for static assets and ALB/EC2 for dynamic or application-backed responses. S3 is ideal for public static files like images, C S S, and H T M L because objects are immutable and safe to cache long-term. For S3 origins, configure Origin Access Control so the bucket denies public access and only CloudFront can fetch objects. ALB or EC2 origins are appropriate for APIs or dynamic content that require server-side computation or personalization. When using ALB/EC2, CloudFront fetches via the origin's public endpoint and you must decide what to forward — query strings, headers, and cookies — so the origin can respond correctly. A useful comparison: S3 origin with long TTLs reduces origin calls and is simple to secure with OAC; ALB/EC2 origin needs careful header forwarding and often short TTLs. A misconception is that S3 cannot serve dynamic content — it can only serve static files; dynamic responses must come from compute origins. Concrete example: host index. html and assets in S3, and point A P I paths to an ALB; enforce OAC on the S3 bucket to prevent direct access. The right origin choice helps you balance performance, security, and freshness.

To reason about performance and origin load, trace the request lifecycle. Step one: DNS resolves the distribution domain to an edge location closest to the viewer. Step two: the edge location checks for the requested object in its cache. If the object exists and is not expired, that's a cache hit — CloudFront returns the object immediately and the origin is not contacted. If the object is missing or expired, that's a cache miss — CloudFront forwards the request to the configured origin, possibly running Lambda@Edge on the way, receives the response, caches it according to the behavior's cache policy, and then delivers it to the viewer. Misconfigurations often cause unnecessary misses: forwarding unnecessary headers or query strings fragments the the cache, and setting very short TTLs turns what could be hits into frequent origin requests. Concrete example: a popular image with long TTL becomes a hit at many edges; an A P I endpoint with TTL=0 always misses and queries the origin. Monitoring the cache hit ratio helps you confirm expected behavior. Ask yourself: for each path pattern, do you prefer freshness or origin throttling? That choice determines caching rules.

Lambda@Edge allows you to run small pieces of serverless code at CloudFront edge locations in response to events in the request lifecycle. This can transform requests, add or remove headers, perform A/B testing, or implement custom routing logic before a request reaches your origin. Because the code runs at the edge, you can reduce origin calls and add personalization closer to the user. Operational health of a CloudFront deployment relies on observability and careful invalidation practices. Monitor metrics like cache hit ratio, origin request rate, and edge latency. A low cache hit ratio indicates either excessive forwarding, too many unique cache keys, or inadequate TTLs. Use CloudFront metrics and logs to identify the paths that cause misses and adjust cache policies or behavior rules accordingly. When content changes and must be refreshed before TTL expiry, use invalidation requests to remove objects from edge caches. Let's summarize the most important terms you need to remember. A Content Delivery Network distributes cached content at edge locations to reduce latency and origin load. A CloudFront distribution is the configuration that ties origins to cache behaviors and policies. An origin is the source of your content — for example, an S3 bucket or an ALB. Origin Access Control prevents direct public access to S3 so CloudFront is the only route to objects. These pieces form the foundation of secure and performant content delivery. Keep these definitions in mind when you design distributions: they describe who serves content, who accesses it, and the rules that determine freshness.
